Severe Flooding Disrupts Chemical Supply Chains in El Salvador

Severe flooding has brought substantial disruption to El Salvador’s chemicals industry this week, as persistent heavy rains continue to batter the eastern departments of San Miguel and La Unión. Industry sources report that at least three major chemical production facilities and two key distribution routes remain impacted, with ongoing rainfall hampering both plant operations and logistics networks.

According to the El Salvador Chemical Industry Association (ESCIA), the overflow of the Río Grande de San Miguel has caused significant flooding at the Poliquímicos SA and Quimicom facilities located on the outskirts of San Miguel city. Both plants, which primarily produce industrial solvents and agrochemical inputs, have suspended operations since Sunday due to rising water levels and safety concerns. “Our immediate priority is the safety of our workers and preventing any accidental releases,” said Rosa Méndez, safety manager at Quimicom, adding that the floodwaters are currently at shoulder height in parts of the facility.

ESCIA estimates that the combined daily output loss from the affected plants exceeds 120 tonnes of chemicals, with downstream effects already felt by local distributors and agricultural cooperatives. “We are coordinating closely with emergency services and the Ministry of Environment to monitor the situation. The true scale of the impact will only be clear once the waters recede,” said Luis Ortega, ESCIA’s executive director.

Transport links have also been severely compromised. The Panamericana Highway, which serves as the main route for chemicals shipments from production sites to the port at La Unión, is partially submerged in several low-lying sections. This has forced hauliers to suspend or reroute deliveries, leading to delays of up to 72 hours for bulk and packaged chemicals. “Every hour of delay increases storage costs and creates backlogs at our terminals,” said Ana Castillo, logistics supervisor at DistribuQuim El Salvador. “We’re running low on buffer stocks and are preparing for potential shortages if conditions persist.”

The National Union of Chemical Workers (SINTQUIM) warned that prolonged flooding could threaten jobs if plant shutdowns extend beyond a week. Union spokesperson Mario Escobar called for urgent government support to restore access and protect workers’ incomes. “Our members are worried about the uncertainty. Quick action is needed to clear routes and safeguard the industry’s future,” he said.

With meteorologists forecasting further rainfall in the region over the next 48 hours, industry officials are bracing for continued disruption. ESCIA has urged all operators in flood-prone areas to review emergency protocols and maintain regular communication with authorities until the situation stabilizes.
